The pr: fix: update player test mocks so the web build typechecks again #69. has been unmerged for sometime, it even says This pull request has changes conflicting with the target branch. apps/web/src/pages/ComparePage.spec.tsx apps/web/src/pages/PlayerProfilePage.spec.tsx now.
Diagnose and suggest a way forward.
the description was PRs #52 (player bio fields) and #53 (player comparisons) merged cleanly as text but not as types: each branch's fixtures were written before the other existed. ComparePage.spec's makePlayer predated the bio fields Player now requires, and PlayerProfilePage.spec's SeasonAverages predated the per-game minutes/made/attempted fields the compare work added.
apps/web builds with tsc -b && vite build, so tsc failed and Vite never ran. Cloudflare Pages keeps serving the last successful build on a failed one, which is why the deployed site still showed the bio card from #52 but none of #53's compare link, MPG tile or FTA/G tile.
Fixtures only — no production code changed.

That branch touched the same two fixtures — it had to, because the stat-editing feature reads minutesPerGame, freeThrowsAttemptedPerGame etc., so its author hit the identical missing-field errors and filled them in.
Both #69 and main added the same fields, but with different fixture values, on the same lines:
Fixture	#69	main
minutesPerGame	35.2	34.5
fieldGoalsMadePerGame / Attempted	10.4 / 20	9.9 / 19
threesMadePerGame / Attempted	1.9 / 5	2.1 / 5.5
freeThrowsMadePerGame / Attempted	4.5 / 6	5.4 / 7.2

    • PlayerProfilePage.tsx:198, :235, :311 — the Compare link, MPG tile and FTA/G tile are all present

Recommended way forward
Close #69 as already-fixed. Don't resolve the conflict — merging it would only churn fixture numbers with no behavioural change, and you'd be re-litigating values that main's tests already assert against. Suggested closing note:
Fixed on main by 23d4062 (#81), which completed the same fixtures while adding local stat editing. Verified: tsc -b clean and both spec files green on main. Closing as superseded — no conflict resolution needed.
Then delete fix-web-build-mocks locally and on origin.

Nothing salvageable in it. Main already has the fix, verified green.
A branch for Age — yes, and it's small
But this isn't a bug, and that matters for how you file it. ComparePage.tsx:79 is a hardcoded placeholder:
// Age needs Player.birthDate, which only exists on the unmerged player
// bio branch — the row is here so it lights up the moment that lands,
// and the page subheading explains the dash until then.
{ label: "Age", render: () => NO_VALUE },
Age never worked on compare. It was deliberately deferred, and the bio branch it was waiting on (#52) has since merged — so it's unblocked scope, not something that broke. This was recorded as deferred at merge time, with the note that the row needs only its render wired to birthDate. That Age now renders on the profile page also tells you the bio backfill has run in production, which was the other caveat hanging over this.
The bug tracker part — file it, but not as bug
By your own label definitions this fits neither type:
    • bug — "Something works differently from how it should"
    • regression — "Used to work; a change broke it"
Filing your tracker's first-ever issue under a label that contradicts its own description is a bad precedent for a scheme you just designed carefully. The real gap: your label set has no type label for new work at all. There's documentation and now bug, but nothing for a feature or enhancement. I'd add enhancement to scripts/setup-gitea-labels.mjs before filing — you'll want it for the O/D rebound split too, and for most of what's left in the backlog.
The user-visible symptom is still worth tracking — "Age shows a dash on compare but a real value on the profile" is exactly the inconsistency someone would report. It's the label that's wrong, not the filing.

Team Git Workflow
Standard git workflow for team projects. Applies any time Claude is helping with git operations — commits, branches, merges, PRs — on a team codebase.
Branches
    • main — the stable, always-up-to-date version of the code. Nothing goes here until it's reviewed and agreed on.
    • Feature branches — one per feature (e.g. a new page, a new endpoint). Branch off main.
        ◦ Examples: applicant-profile-page, cv-upload, nqf-dropdown
        ◦ Keep names short, lowercase, hyphenated.
Committing
Always ask before committing. Never run git commit (or git push) without first showing the proposed commit message(s) and getting an explicit go-ahead. This applies even if the work is clearly finished.
One commit per independent unit of work. A unit of work is a single feature, a single bug fix, a single refactor, etc. — things that don't depend on each other. If a change touches two unrelated things, split it into two commits (and ask about each separately if needed). Don't bundle "add CV upload" and "fix typo in nav" into one commit.
Scoped commits, simple humanized tags. Format:
tag: short plain-English description
    • Tag is one lowercase word, no parentheses/scopes (skip feat(auth): style — keep it simple)
    • Common tags: feat, fix, refactor, chore, docs, style, test
    • Description is imperative, no trailing period: feat: add CV upload button, not feat: Added CV upload button.
    • No walls of text in the subject line — if more detail is needed, put it in the commit body, not the tag line Examples:
    • feat: add NQF qualification dropdown
    • fix: correct SAQA lookup validation
    • refactor: simplify applicant form state
    • chore: bump supabase client version
Checking for sensitive info before committing
Before proposing any commit, check the staged changes for secrets or sensitive data — don't just trust .gitignore. Look for things like:
    • API keys, tokens, or credentials (e.g. Supabase service role keys, JWT secrets)
    • .env files or hardcoded connection strings/passwords
    • Private keys or certificates (.pem, .key, etc.)
    • Any personal data that shouldn't be in the repo Practically:
    1. Run git diff --staged (or check git status for files about to be added) and scan it yourself before writing the commit message.
    2. If something sensitive shows up, stop and flag it — don't commit it, and suggest moving it to a .env file (added to .gitignore) or an untracked config file instead.
    3. If a secret has already been committed in an earlier commit, flag that separately — removing it from the latest commit isn't enough, it's still in git history and the key should be rotated.
Merging back to main
Only merge a feature branch into main once all team members have reviewed the code and agree it's good and finished. Before merging:
    1. Confirm the branch has actually been reviewed (don't assume — ask the user if the team has signed off).
    2. If there's no confirmation that everyone agrees, don't merge — flag it and suggest opening/continuing a PR for review instead.
Quick workflow summary
    1. Branch off main for the feature.
    2. Do the work.
    3. When a self-contained unit of work is done, check the staged changes for secrets/sensitive info, then propose a commit message using the tag format above and ask before committing.
    4. Push the feature branch.
    5. Open for team review (PR or equivalent).
    6. Merge to main only once everyone has reviewed and agreed it's finished.

Coding Conventions
Apply these conventions when writing or reviewing code.
Design
    • Follow SOLID object-oriented design principles where applicable: Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, Dependency Inversion.
Naming
    • Variables are nouns. Prefer elapsed_time_in_days = 0 over d = 0.
    • Functions are verbs. Prefer update_item_price() over item_updater().
    • Avoid disinformation. Don't name something in a way that misrepresents what it is — e.g. don't call a list an "array", don't name a variable accountList if it's actually a Map.
    • Include units of measurement in variable names when the variable measures something. Prefer time_in_milliseconds over time.
Functions
    • Keep functions small. Each function should do one thing, contain few lines, and prefer a single level of indentation. Treat this as a strong preference, not a hard limit — don't over-extract trivial one-line helpers just to satisfy the rule.
General
    • Avoid magic numbers and strings. Use named constants instead of unexplained literals.
    • Use consistent casing per language convention — e.g. snake_case for Python, camelCase for JavaScript/Java — matching the idiomatic style of the language in use.
Documentation
    • Document code as it's written, not after. Add docstrings/comments in the same pass as writing the function, not as a cleanup step later.
    • Be descriptive about how functions work — explain what the function does, its parameters, return value, and any non-obvious behavior or edge cases, not just a one-line restatement of the function name.
CRUD Methodology
    • Adhere to CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) methodology when designing functions and data-handling code. Each function should map clearly to one of these operations rather than mixing several — e.g. keep create_user(), get_user(), update_user(), and delete_user() as separate functions instead of one function that both creates and updates records.

Confirmed — comparePlayers calls the same getPlayerById the profile page uses, so both pages already received identical Player objects. Here's the description:
## What was wrong

The Age row on `/compare` rendered a dash for every player, while the same
player's profile page showed a real age.

The cause was a placeholder that was never flipped. When the compare page was
built (#53), `Player.birthDate` did not exist yet — it was still on the
unmerged player bio branch. The Age row was written to hold its place:

```ts
// Age needs Player.birthDate, which only exists on the unmerged player
// bio branch — the row is here so it lights up the moment that lands,
// and the page subheading explains the dash until then.
{ label: "Age", render: () => NO_VALUE },
```

The bio branch merged the day before as #52, but nothing came back to this row,
so it kept returning a hardcoded dash regardless of the data.

Two things made it read as a bug rather than as unfinished work:

- **The profile page worked.** #52 shipped its own `calculateAge` alongside the
  bio fields, so age rendered correctly there from day one. The two pages
  disagreeing about the same player looked like something broken.
- **The data was already arriving.** `GET /v1/players/compare` builds each entry
  with the same `getPlayerById` that `GET /v1/players/:id` uses, so the compare
  page was receiving `birthDate` in full and throwing it away at render time.

`calculateAge` was also a private, unexported function inside
`PlayerProfilePage.tsx`, so the compare page had no way to reach it even if
someone had gone looking.

## What this changes

**Extracted the shared bio formatting into `apps/web/src/lib/playerBio.ts`** —
`calculateAge`, `formatAge`, `formatHeight` and the shared `NO_VALUE` dash.
`calculateAge` moved across unchanged. `formatHeight` was already duplicated
in both pages, so this collapses an existing copy rather than adding a layer.

**Wired the Age row to `player.birthDate`** and removed the stale placeholder
comment.

**Removed the subheading's "Age arrives once player bios land"** — it had become
a promise about work that was already done, and would have read as a lie the
moment the row populated.

**`PlayerProfilePage` now imports both helpers** instead of keeping its own
copies. No behaviour change there.

No API, schema or ingestion changes — this is a render fix on data the endpoint
was already returning.

## Notes for review

- **Age deliberately has no `compareValue`.** Every other row highlights a
  leader; there is no better age to be, so this row stays unhighlighted.
- **The two pages still treat a missing bio differently.** The profile page
  distinguishes "not ingested yet" from "genuinely absent" via `isBioLoaded` and
  shows "Loading…"; the compare page has no such concept and shows a dash.
  Porting that across felt like scope beyond this fix — worth a follow-up if the
  team wants them consistent.

## Testing

- New `playerBio.spec.ts` — 10 cases against a frozen clock, covering the
  birthday-today and birthday-tomorrow boundaries and the null-`birthDate` path.
- New compare-page test asserting both players' ages render for real bios.
- Updated the existing dash-count test's comment, which claimed "Age has no
  source on this branch".
- Full web suite: 131 passed / 24 files. `tsc -b` and `vite build` both clean.
